If you cut the wall and patch it invisibly, and he later finds out, he can argue you damaged the property *and* tampered with evidence. A visible, documented cut that you told him about in writing ("I am cutting an inspection port to verify mold per health dept. guidance") is actually more legally defensible than a hidden one.

## If you still want to open the wall

Here's how to do it cleanly. This is standard drywall repair work:

**Tools:** drywall saw or oscillating multi-tool, utility knife, stud finder, flashlight, phone camera, N95 mask (important - disturbing mold aerosolizes spores), gloves, plastic sheeting.

**The cut:**
1. Kill power to any nearby outlets at the breaker. Check for pipes with the stud finder.
2. Tape plastic around the area to contain spores.
3. Cut a clean rectangle - roughly 6x8" is enough to photograph and swab. Make cuts along a straightedge so the patch sits flush. Bevel the cut slightly inward so the piece can drop back in.
4. Photograph with flash and without; get a swab sample into a ziplock for a cheap mail-in mold test ($30-50, results in a week).

**The patch:**
1. Cut two small wood backer strips (1x2 or plywood scraps), slip them behind the hole, screw through the surrounding drywall into them.
2. Screw your cut piece into the backers.
3. Apply fiberglass mesh tape over the seams.
4. Three coats of joint compound, each wider than the last (roughly 6", 10", 14"), sanding between coats with 220 grit. Feather the edges.
5. Prime with a stain-blocking primer (Kilz or similar - important because any residual moisture will bleed through).
6. Paint - and here's the catch: unless you have the exact paint and it's aged the same way, the patch will show as a slightly different sheen or color in raking light. Painting the whole wall corner-to-corner hides this best.

Done well, a patch is invisible head-on but often visible at an angle in certain light. A week isn't much cure time - joint compound can still look faintly different even after priming.

**One more thought:** the health department route genuinely is faster and doesn't put your deposit (or your legal position) at risk. If you haven't called them yet, try that first this week.
